#10363. Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

New workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. 

As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work.  

That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations. 

When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. 

Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t. 

A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations.

While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption. 

Only 39% of users have built AI into a standardized way of working, according to the LSE Inclusion Initiative and Protiviti report. Those who have reported saving 27% of time in their work week with AI, compared with 14% for those who haven’t. 

Gen Z is far more likely to have been AI-trained in the past year compared with their baby boomer colleagues. AI-trained employees report saving 22% of their working hours, compared with 13% for those left to figure it out alone. 

And what exactly happens to all that extra time saved by AI? More time for more work, of course. And it’s causing what researchers are calling “workload creep”. 

“AI is creating meaningful productivity gains, but the bigger opportunity is how organizations use the capacity it creates,” said Matt Duncan, managing director at Protiviti, in the press release. “Simply absorbing those gains into existing workloads leaves much of AI’s potential untapped.”

Researchers at Boston Consulting Group found that 14% of people who use AI workflows requiring a high degree of oversight experience “AI brain fry.” This mental fog and inability to focus can result in more mistakes at work, and even employees considering quitting altogether. 

AI or not, job performance is still dependent on people, at least for now. And the LSE and Protiviti report found no consistent association between an employee’s perceived performance and their AI adoption, access, training or workflow integration. Instead, performance stayed tied to confidence in solving problems, conscientiousness, resilience and willingness to learn.

As AI continues to become embedded in everyday work, organizations need to focus on whether it is actually helping employees be more efficient at work, or simply creating time to pile more work on their plates. 

“Leaders should think deliberately about where that capacity can create the most value, whether that means tackling higher-value work, improving quality or giving employees greater space to solve problems and innovate,” said Duncan. 

“The goal shouldn’t just be doing more work faster, but using AI to change what people are able to accomplish.”

#10360. Is Kling 4.0 the Right AI Video Generator for Your Project?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

This article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you plan a production.

● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

Most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

If you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

If you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

Use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly shows what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

No single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Kling’s own site is the place to check announcements and API options directly, since its page says little about durations or resolution. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

Trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

Making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project update a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

Generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4

Because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

If people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

Think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

This matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a new generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

The Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP currently offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you plan to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

Decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

● Read the licence. JXP’s page lists a commercial use license on each plan and says outputs are for creative and lawful use, with the user responsible for reviewing them. Other tools have different terms.

● Use inputs you have the right to use. Do not upload other people’s copyrighted work or photos of people without permission.

● Do not misrepresent products or events. A generated clip should not suggest features or footage that do not exist.

● Consider provenance. C2PA is an open standard for Content Credentials that records where content came from and how it was edited, and some tools support it.

● Disclose where required. Follow platform and advertising rules on labelling AI-generated or altered content.

● Fine text, logos, hands and fast motion can drift or flicker between frames.

● Reference images and keyframes steer the result but do not guarantee an exact match.

● Vendor specifications, such as resolution and length, can differ between a model announcement and a particular platform.

● Credit costs and plan terms change, so check them on the day you generate.

● Long or exact sequences are often cheaper and safer to film than to generate.

Short imagined shots, concept clips and moving backgrounds, where some details can be left open and the clip is reviewed before use.

Use text when you only have an idea, reference mode when you have a picture or clip to guide the look, and keyframes when specific views matter at specific moments.

Not reliably. Use real footage or a screen recording for instructions and demonstrations.

No. Hosted studios, vendor sites, developer APIs and open-source pipelines all exist. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your project.

Kling 4.0 is a good candidate when the missing piece is an imagined shot and you can describe what it needs to do. Pick one such shot, try it, and put it next to the material you already have, and compare at least one alternative before you commit. If the project needs exact instructions or a faithful record, use the real thing. A useful first result is one that does its job in the edit, not simply one that looks impressive on its own.

#10358. Are AI companies ‘glosslighting’ you with misleading jargon? This report says yes

Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “copilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry.

“Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades.

Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice takes on extra weight.

What is glosslighting?

For the study, researchers at the university in British Columbia analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion.

The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. 

“Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,’” the authors write.

How AI jargon causes harm

The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following:

  • “Hallucination,” “copilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them.
  • “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development.
  • “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns.
  • “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy.
  • “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laypeople to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin

The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go in depth to provide greater accuracy to descriptions of AI’s impact.

One author, Nicholas Vincent, an assistant professor of computing science, told Tech Xplore that “issues where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.”

“Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”

#10356. AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.

Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has announced additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns.

Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him.

Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN.

The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses.

Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait?

Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it.

“AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.”

AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology.

THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM

Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker.

Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise?

Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players.

“Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub says. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.”

Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products.

“The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.”

That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on.

In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices.

Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing.

“The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says.

She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning.

“I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says.

For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations.

Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance.

THE BILL IS COMING DUE

Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology.

Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save.

“The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.”

Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive.

Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost.

Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified.

The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive.

Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with.

“Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company.

This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models?

Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow.

“I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.”

WHO GETS THE VALUE?

Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software.

Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods.

“There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.”

His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient.

“Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?”

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says.

Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

“The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary.

A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”

He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

“For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

#10354. Can potential clients find you using AI?

A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.” 

If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website.

Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time.

AI as the new recommendation engine

For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did.

AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. 

In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers said they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a big jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for.

Make sure you have a consistent online presence

Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results.

You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. 

Your website

Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find.

From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better.

Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course).

Your content on other sites

Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well.

Claim your business profile

Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary.

In November 2026, OpenAI launched a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can update its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website.

A LinkedIn Company Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it shows up when people search on LinkedIn.

AI is one more way people ask for information

I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also plan to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (currently sitting at 19).

Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

#10352. Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.

Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.

A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS, based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents said letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced.

Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI. Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort.

There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes.

That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit they’re struggling. The report found that 45% of respondents had avoided questioning a new way of working because they didn’t want to appear resistant. Among those who continued to use, or fell back on, old ways of working, 22% said they feared making mistakes or looking slow.

When workplaces demand this constant adaptation without creating the space for it, employees might prefer to stick to what they know. Sixty percent said their workplace prioritized results over the process of getting them, while just 41% said they felt they were given room to be less productive while learning something new.

There may also be a question of trust. Employees who have seen workplace initiatives and technologies come and go may be reluctant to embrace the latest change, particularly if they aren’t convinced it will last. They may prefer to future-proof themselves by leaning on the skills and systems they already know, rather than investing time in learning a new tool that could be forgotten about in six months.

That reluctance could be costing employers: The report found that 29% of employees said their company was investing in tools they’d stopped using.

But habit hugging isn’t necessarily an outright rejection of change. The report found that 73% of respondents mixed old and new ways of working to get the job done, suggesting employees may be finding ways to adapt without abandoning familiar routines altogether.

Rather than blindly embracing the latest systems, people may be finding their own ways of adapting to a future nobody is sure of.

#10349. How job hunting became an expensive cash suck

There’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. 

We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. 

Char, who lives in the UK, said the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive.

“I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.” 

And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. 

In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent.

Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt.

“Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said.


Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack up. 

The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket.

An Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% said they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview.

Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) said current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site.

Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue.

Work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

#10348. How Consumer AI Companions Handle Context Windows, Persistent Memory, and Voice Latency

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI companions are the most demanding consumer use of large language models right now. A coding assistant can forget your last message and still be useful. A companion that forgets your name, your running story, or the plan you made last Tuesday has failed at its one job. On top of that, users now expect voice calls that feel like a phone conversation, not a walkie-talkie exchange with a five-second pause.

Three engineering problems decide whether a companion app works: how much of the conversation fits in the model's context window, what the app remembers once the window fills up, and how fast the voice pipeline answers. Here is how consumer companions handle each one, with real tier and pricing examples, and what developers can take from their designs for their own products.

Most LLM products are judged on single answers. Companions are judged on continuity. That creates pressure in three places at once:

Every consumer companion is a different set of trade-offs across those three constraints, and the trade-offs are increasingly how the apps are priced.

The context window is the total number of tokens the model can see when it writes the next reply. In a companion app, that budget is spent before the user says anything:

When the chat log outgrows what is left, the oldest messages fall out. The user experiences this as the companion "forgetting" mid-conversation. This is why context size is now a headline spec in the category, and a paid feature. SpicyChat AI, for example, gives free accounts a 4K context window, then scales memory to 8K on its $19.95/mo tier and 32K on its $29.95/mo tier. Janitor AI runs about 9K of context on its own JanitorLLM. Independent uncensored AI chat benchmarks record these context sizes alongside refusal behavior and pricing, because context length predicts how long a roleplay stays coherent better than any marketing claim.

Some apps sell memory in messages rather than tokens. Fantasy GF's pricing page lists a 60-message base "smart memory" and 5x that, 300 messages, on its Ultra plan. Others sell it as a memory multiplier on higher subscription tiers. The pattern is consistent across the category: memory depth is the upgrade lever, not the model itself.

No consumer app keeps an entire relationship in the prompt. Persistent memory is a separate system that writes to storage and reads back into the context window on each turn. In practice it has three layers:

The differences users notice are usually retention policies, not algorithms. Crushon AI's own subscription docs say free-plan chat history is deleted after 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans keep it for the membership period. Paid tiers across the category commonly promise that memories never expire. There is also a security angle worth stating plainly: companion chat logs are among the most sensitive data a consumer product can hold. A 2024 breach at Muah.ai, first reported by 404 Media, exposed roughly 1.9 million users' email addresses together with their private prompts. Any app that builds persistent memory is also building a liability, and developers copying the pattern should treat the memory store as the most protected part of the system.

A voice call in a companion app is three models chained together: speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech. Run them strictly in sequence and a single reply can take several seconds, which reads as dead air. The apps that feel fast attack each stage the same way:

With every stage streaming, time-to-first-audio can land close to a second on a good connection, which is roughly the threshold where a conversation stops feeling laggy. Voice is also expensive to run - three model calls instead of one, plus audio bandwidth - which is why it is metered harder than text. Fantasy GF charges 8 tokens per minute for voice calls (4 on Ultra), which turns the 100 monthly tokens on its entry plan into about 12 minutes of call time. SpicyChat, for its part, only adds text-to-speech at its top tier. Latency engineering and unit economics are the same problem here: faster pipelines cost less per call, and cheaper calls are what make voice viable below the top plan.

Tier details below come from each app's own pricing or documentation pages, checked November 16, 2026, and cross-checked against il.ly's AI companion testing guide, which hands-tests 15 companion apps across memory, media, and voice.

Two takeaways from the table. First, nobody sells a bigger base model - they sell a bigger window into the same one. Second, the free tiers are deliberately memory-poor: limited context and short retention are the upgrade prompt.

Even if you never build a companion, these apps are a useful reference architecture for any stateful LLM product:

Consumer AI companions have turned three hard infrastructure problems - bounded context, durable memory, and real-time voice - into their pricing pages. Context size, memory depth, and voice access are the tiers. If you are building anything stateful on an LLM, this category is worth watching closely: it is solving continuity and latency problems at consumer scale, in public, one subscription tier at a time.

It is the total amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider when writing its next reply. The character definition, stored memories, recent chat, and the new message all share that budget. When the conversation exceeds it, the oldest content drops out and the companion appears to forget.

Yes, through a memory system separate from the context window. Apps summarize older chats, extract stable facts about you into a profile, and retrieve relevant past moments into the prompt. Retention varies: some free tiers delete chat history after as little as 7 days of inactivity, while paid plans typically keep memory for the membership period.

A voice turn runs three models - speech-to-text, the LLM, and text-to-speech - instead of one, plus audio transfer. Providers pass that cost on through per-minute token charges or by locking voice behind higher tiers.

For casual chat, 4K to 9K tokens works. For long-running roleplay or a companion expected to hold plot threads for weeks, 32K and up, or a well-built memory layer on top of a smaller window, makes the visible difference.

#10347. Here’s the best day to shop for travel deals—and it isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday

Black Friday may have come early this year, but the best travel deals are still to come, according to data from Skyscanner—which found the best day to find discounts on travel isn’t Black Friday or Travel Tuesday.

While Travel Tuesday generates plenty of buzz, Skyscanner analyzed billions of proprietary flight data points and found Cyber Monday was the cheapest day to book flights. That day had “the lowest average price per seat” across the five-day Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday sales period last year, according to Skyscanner, a global travel platform.

“Cyber Monday offered the lowest average fares, making it a day worth checking this year,” Lourdes Losada, Skyscanner’s director of the Americas, tells Fast Company. “Start comparing fares before the sales begin so you have a baseline, then monitor prices throughout the period. Knowing what your flight typically costs makes it easier to recognize a worthwhile offer without feeling pressured by a sale’s countdown.”

However, Travel Tuesday still had plenty of standout destination-specific savings, with average flights to Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Seoul; and Honolulu dropping 28%, 24%, and 15% respectively, compared with the previous 12-month average. This is an indication that there are strong deals across the entire period.

The destination that saw the largest surge in interest was Cabo San Lucas, the Mexican resort town in Baja California Sur. Searches for the location increased 444% across the full Black Friday-to-Travel Tuesday window, compared with the previous 12-month average.

Other destinations that Americans searched for on Travel Tuesday included Florence, Italy (interest up 163%); Edinburgh, Scotland (up 162%); Liberia (up 158%), Hanoi, Vietnam (up 147%); and Tokyo (up 132%).

Where did American travelers find the biggest Black Friday and Travel Tuesday deals? For travelers looking for savings by destination, the biggest average flight price drops were for Casablanca, Morocco (-30%); Lisbon, Portugal (-28%); Sydney (-21%); Seoul (-17%); and Honolulu (-16%). 

Skyscanner’s advice for shopping the deals

Skyscanner recommends travelers be flexible with dates, set a price alert, stay open to new destinations, and check for alternative departure or arrival airports near your home and destination.

The key takeaway is that travelers shouldn’t feel pressure to book on one day, since the entire five-day window provides opportunities that might otherwise be missed, according to Skyscanner.

“Black Friday can bring a lot of tempting travel offers and it can also be an overwhelming time to book,” says Laura Lindsay, travel trends and destination expert at Skyscanner. “The key is not to rush, stay open minded and focus on the trip that works best for your budget and plans.”

#10346. Nvidia proves it’s too big to fail

Good morning. Today I’m deciding whether the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer passes the “people just standing around” test, trying the new Material 3 Expressive Claude app on my Android devices, and stocking up on discounted XTEINK e-readers for Christmas gifts.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

Eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also said input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

As recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the company had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed quickly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the new Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

Nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the company’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

I was pretty gobsmacked when I saw the news of Huang’s return come across the wire at 9am ET yesterday. I’m still wrapping my head around it. Is Nvidia too big to fail, or just a symptom of a larger interdependency between the US executive branch and Big Tech? Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.

Better-tasting water for your morning coffee, everyday cooking, or a house full of holiday guests? Waterdrop Filter’s Black Friday sale has options for all three, from high-capacity under-sink reverse osmosis systems to installation-free countertop models. Upgrade your kitchen with the X12 under-sink system for $899, save space with the compact G6A6 for $189.99, or skip the plumbing with the M6HG countertop system for $299, which delivers filtered hot water for coffee and tea in seconds.

Whichever setup fits your routine, use code 9TO5GBF26 to take an extra 5% off those sale prices. Waterdrop’s offers also extend to whole-home filtration and replacement refrigerator filters, giving you plenty of ways to upgrade without stretching your holiday budget. Shop Waterdrop’s Black Friday deals on Amazon before the sale ends November 30th.

Since it’s Black Friday week, I figured I’d round up some of the best deals we’ve found so far.

A discounted Pixel: The Pixel 10 at $600 is a really good deal. Recent software updates have closed some of the feature gaps with the Pixel 11, and the hardware is still solid even a year after launch. If you want better cameras, the Pixel 11 Pro at $749 is an absolute steal.

The gaming-tablet deal: The Legion Tab Gen 5 at $599 makes much more sense than it did at $899: an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, a 12GB/256GB configuration, and an included folio. It’s a good fit for someone specifically seeking a compact Android gaming machine.

The last-generation watch: The 40mm Galaxy Watch 8 at $199 is the sort of older smartwatch worth considering when annual upgrades are modest. And because the Watch 9 is basically identical, I’d go for the Watch 8. If you are looking at Samsung’s latest and greatest, the Galaxy Watch 9 is $379 with a free $50 Amazon gift card, which is a decent deal, too.

A deal on the year’s best Android foldable: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is showing up at $1,499.99 for some lucky shoppers and $1,549.99 for the rest. Either way, it’s Samsung’s best product of 2026, and my current favorite gadget.

Google’s latest mid-sized sedan AI model is taking the world by storm. Gemini 4 Neon is technically the middle sibling in Google’s lineup, with Carbon at the top and Hydrogen at the bottom, but everyone seems to agree it absolutely cooks.

If you’ve spent any time on X over the past few days (I hate myself for writing that), you’ll likely have seen an uptick in fervor over Google’s latest model, which seems to outperform Claude Opus 5.5, and even Gemini 4 Carbon itself, in many benchmarks and real-world tests. Even Google is providing some helpful guidance about when to use one or the other.

One thing I’ve read again and again about Neon is how adept it is at writing. I’m of two minds about this: the better an AI gets at doing my job, the less necessary I am at said job. On the other hand, I’m so tired of obvious AI slop that a model that actually writes well sounds like a relief. At least when I’m unemployed, I won’t be yelling at the screen all day about why the robot yet again used negative parallelism.

I didn’t get to play much GTA VI over the weekend, but I know a few (million) people who did. Publisher Take-Two says the game generated $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. That’s an incredible number in any industry, but a truly mind-blowing one in the video game world. Rockstar also released its first patch for the game on Monday to fix a modest number of bugs with the launch code.

If you follow open-weight AI models, you’ll likely have heard of how influential Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 was when it launched in June. Now the company has released GLM-5.4, and it’s novel as much for its architecture as it is for its benchmarks.

Its Loop Transformer reuses a block of layers to do more computation without adding parameters. The company is pitching applications beyond software, including games, visual work, and CAD. The 750-million-parameter model reportedly performs at the level of a 2-3 trillion parameter non-looping equivalent, but we’re still waiting on a broader release for real-world testing.

In browser news, Ladybird’s first public alpha is now downloadable for macOS and Linux. It’s built with a brand-new engine that eschews many of the legacy decisions made by Google’s Chromium team. And the project has the backing of big names like Shopify, Cloudflare, and Proton. It’s still pretty rough, and features are paltry, but any new competition in the browser space is a win in my book.

#10344. Are stores open on Thanksgiving Day 2026? Holiday hours for Walmart, Whole Foods, Costco, and more

Thanksgiving centers on gratitude, which is good for mental health, as scientific studies have proven.

The stress and anxiety of the holiday season can almost seem antithetical to these findings. It’s hard to be zen when wondering if the local supermarket is open because you need another cup of milk for the mashed potatoes.

Here’s everything you need to know about what is open and closed on Thanksgiving for those last-minute needs. We even threw in some fun facts so you can wow everyone at dinner with your wit and wisdom. 

Do other countries celebrate Thanksgiving?

The United States is not the only country that celebrates gratitude at the end of the year.

The first recorded Canadian Thanksgiving took place in 1578, which was more than 40 years before its American counterpart. In Canada, Thanksgiving takes place on the second Monday in October.

In Germany, Erntedankfest, a harvest of thanks, takes place in September or October, depending on the year.

In Japan, Kinro Kansha no Hi, Labor Thanksgiving Day, focuses on appreciation for workers. This celebration evolved from an ancient rice festival and takes place on November 23.

In Liberia, Thanksgiving falls on the first Thursday of November. A spicy roast chicken is the main dish, not turkey.

Is Thanksgiving a federal holiday?

Yes. In the United States, Thanksgiving takes place on the fourth Thursday of November and is a federal holiday.

Are banks open on Thanksgiving?

No, most are closed for the holiday, as is the Federal Reserve. Online banking and ATMs outside branches are good alternatives.

Is the stock market open on Thanksgiving?

No. Even the stock market takes a day off to be grateful for capital gains. Both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are closed.

Is the Post Office open on Thanksgiving? Is Mail delivered?

Unless you are getting your Hogwarts acceptance letter by owl, no mail will be delivered on Thanksgiving.

Physical post office locations operated by the U.S. Postal Service will be closed for the holiday. Online services and self-serve kiosks are your best bet in a pinch.

Are FedEx and UPS delivering on Thanksgiving?

No, FedEx locations are not open and it is not delivering or picking up on Thanksgiving.

Most UPS locations are also closed and the organization is not delivering or picking up. The only exception is UPS Express Critical service. 

Are schools open on Thanksgiving?

No. The majority of schools will not be in session due to the holiday. It is always a good practice to double-check with your child’s institution.

Are restaurants open on Thanksgiving?

Yes. Many restaurants will be open. Some will even feature a special menu for the holiday as certain families would rather make reservations than a turkey with all the trimmings.

Are retail stores open on Thanksgiving?

Only some retail stores will be open on Thanksgiving. Walmart, Target, REI, Kohl’s, Dick’s Sporting Goods, and Home Depot are just some of the chains that will be closed.

It is probably safer to focus on turkey instead of shopping on Thanksgiving. On Black Friday, however, all bets are off.

Are pharmacies open on Thanksgiving?

Some pharmacies will remain open on Thanksgiving. For instance, more than 4,000 Walgreens locations will be open. It is best to double-check your favorite location before you head out so you avoid getting headaches, even if they are just metaphorical ones.

Are grocery stores open on Thanksgiving?

Only some grocery stores are open on Thanksgiving. Do not go to Costco, Trader Joe’s, Sam’s Club, Aldi or Publix for last-minute meal supplies as you will find closed doors.

Kroger says stores will be open until 4 p.m. Whole Foods says most stores are open with modified hours, so check your local location.

What television specials are happening on Thanksgiving?

Since 1924, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been delighting spectators with its big balloons, floats, and musical acts.

This year marks its 100th iteration (No parades took place from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II)). However, the parade will be postponed for the first time in its history. New York City is under a high-wind warning due to a nor’easter.

New balloons joining in on the milestone celebration include Bluey, Hello Kitty, Joe Cool and Woodstock, and Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey.

Natasha Bedingfield, Devo, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Mckenna Grace, Megan Moroney, Indigo Girls, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, Smash Mouth, and Teddy Swims are just some of the performers lending their talents to the parade route.

One controversial change is a single 10-minute Broadway medley featuring performers from nine Broadway shows. Historically, several shows have been able to perform their own numbers.

The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is broadcast on NBC on Saturday, November 28, from 8:30 a.m. to 12 noon, across all time zones. It will also be available to stream on Peacock.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When one person chats with a local model, it barely matters which server you run. On one RTX 3090 with the same model file, Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp wrote text within about 10 percent of each other, because all three run llama.cpp underneath. That changes when your app sends several requests at once. With four requests, the best setup produced more than three times as much text as the worst, and the cause was a default setting, not the engine. With 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times as much text as the best llama.cpp setup I tested.

This article puts those numbers side by side and shows which setting to change for your app.

I ran every test on one machine. The full write-ups, with every command and the raw results, are on homebrewserver.club.

Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp loaded the exact same GGUF files, checked by SHA-256. vLLM cannot run GGUF files well, so it loaded a 4-bit AWQ file of the same model (9.1 GB). Answer quality was not compared.

The tests ran between 8 and 16 November 2026, and speeds on this machine varied by a few percent from one day to the next. Treat a gap under about 5% as a tie. All of this is one consumer GPU and one model family, so read the numbers as a guide to how the servers behave, not as a ranking for your hardware.

This is the short prompt with a 512-token answer.

Ollama and LM Studio both start llama.cpp's llama-server program for each model they load. Ollama has done this since version 0.30, and a comment in its source code says so. On Linux, LM Studio's CUDA runtime is a folder with llama.cpp libraries and a llama-server binary.

Ollama logs the command it starts when you set OLLAMA_DEBUG=1. When llama.cpp was started by hand with that exact command, in a run next to Ollama, its speed matched Ollama's within 1%. So Ollama adds no speed cost of its own. LM Studio was 5 to 10% slower in this test. The test did not separate whether that came from its llama.cpp build or its other start options.

For one user, the gap between Ollama and LM Studio was about 0.4 s on a 512-token answer from the 9B model. You would notice it in long answers, and hardly in a chat window.

A web app rarely sends one request at a time. A chat page, a background summary job and an agent can all call the same model at the same moment. The next test sent four requests at once, each asking for 256 tokens, and measured the total output per second.

A slot is one request that the server works on at the same time as others. llama-server sets the number of slots with -np (short for --parallel), and Ollama and LM Studio pass their own setting through to it.

With one slot, the server answers the four requests one after another, so the total stays at the speed of a single request. That is Ollama's default. With four slots, the server puts the four requests through the model together, and the total rose to more than twice that of one slot. That is the default in LM Studio and llama.cpp. vLLM was the fastest at four requests, but it was tested only with the 9B model. Its lead grows with more requests, as the section after next shows.

For your app, this means that the fourth user of a default Ollama server waits for the first three answers to finish before their own answer starts.

The obvious fix is OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4. It worked for the 9B model, though in one of three rounds Ollama still answered at the speed of a single request. With the 27B model, it made Ollama slower than its default.

The cause is how each server sizes the context, the memory that holds each request's prompt and answer. Ollama picks the context from the GPU's memory: 32,768 tokens on a 24 GB card, according to its docs. With four slots, it gives each slot its own 32,768 tokens, so it started llama-server with a 131,072-token context. The Ollama FAQ says the memory needed grows with the number of parallel requests multiplied by the context length.

That context did not fit next to the 27B model in 24 GB. ollama ps showed 16% of the model on the CPU, and the total speed fell to 33.1 tokens per second.

LM Studio and llama.cpp handle it differently. Their four slots share one pool of context:

The price of LM Studio's default is a short context. Four requests sharing 8,192 tokens leave little room for long documents or a long chat history. If your app sends long prompts, load the model with a larger context.

In Ollama, setting a smaller context with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH next to OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL should avoid the spill to the CPU. The test did not try this, so measure it on your own card.

The last test went further, from 1 to 32 requests at once, with the 9B model. It compared vLLM, a server built to serve one model to many users, with llama.cpp at its defaults and with more slots. Ollama and LM Studio were tested only up to four requests, so they are not in this table.

With its defaults, llama-server chose four slots by itself, so it worked on four requests and queued the rest. Its total stayed near 330 tokens per second from 4 requests to 32. Setting -np 16 or -np 32 roughly doubled the total at 16 requests.

vLLM's lead came from each request running faster inside a large batch. At 32 requests, each vLLM request generated about 61 tokens per second, against about 27 on llama.cpp with 32 slots. vLLM's README names the two techniques behind this: PagedAttention, which stores each request's working memory in small blocks, and continuous batching, which adds new requests to the batch the GPU is already working on.

Total output tells you how much work the server does. The wait for the first word tells you how the app feels to the user behind the last request:

For a web app, that is 22.5 seconds of spinner before any text appears. Long prompts make every wait longer, on both servers. With eight requests of about 4,120 tokens each, the last request waited 7.9 s on vLLM and 8.8 s on llama.cpp with 32 slots.

If you set the slots yourself, the llama-server README lists three options that work together:

If you run an older llama.cpp, update first. Four requests at once ran 14 to 22% faster on v1.0.0 than on the build from five days earlier, while one request stayed the same. The most likely reason is a new CUDA kernel in v1.0 for steps of 2 to 24 tokens on RTX 30-series and newer cards.

vLLM's throughput comes with two costs that matter on a shared machine.

It reserves most of the GPU. By default, vLLM takes 92% of the card's memory before it loads anything, and fills what the model does not need with cache. With a desktop and a browser holding about 2 GiB, vLLM refused to start:

Setting --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 alone was not enough with this model, because the default limit of 256 sequences needed more cache than fit. Adding --max-num-seqs 32 fixed it. With both settings, vLLM held 12.7 GiB and kept the same speeds. llama.cpp works the other way: it sizes its cache from -c and -np and never asked for more than 15.1 GiB in this test.

It starts slowly. llama-server answered requests 2 to 5 s after its container started. vLLM compiles the model before it serves anything. That took 72 s with its compile cache already on disk, and 173 s on the first start without it. Changing a vLLM argument triggered a fresh compile.

It also needs a different model file. vLLM loads Hugging Face safetensors, so a 4-bit model is a separate AWQ or GPTQ upload. The AWQ file here was 9.1 GB against 5.7 GB for the GGUF, because its recipe leaves some layers unquantized. Check the file size, not only "4-bit", when you size a model for your card.

All four servers have an OpenAI-compatible API under /v1, so the same client code works with each one. You change the base URL and the model name. These are the ports used in the tests:

In Node.js with the openai package, that looks like the sketch below. The measurements came from a Python test client, and this snippet was not part of them:

Qwen3.5 thinks before it answers unless you turn it off. The tests sent "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} in the request body to vLLM and llama.cpp.

None of the servers asked for a password in these tests. llama-server also warned at start-up that its CORS rule allowed all origins. Bind the port to 127.0.0.1, as in the table, and set --api-key on llama.cpp or vLLM if anything else on your network can reach it.

Before you choose, count how many requests your app really sends at the same moment. Log the timestamps for a day, or count the parallel calls your agent makes per user action. If that number is one, any of these servers will do. If it is four or more, the slot setting will change your users' wait more than the choice of engine.

Not for one request with the same settings. Ollama runs llama.cpp's own server, and the two were within 1% when started with the same command. llama.cpp was faster with four requests at once, because it starts four slots by default and Ollama starts one.

Ollama gives each parallel request its own full context. With four slots on a 24 GB card, that was 131,072 tokens, which pushed 16% of a 27B model onto the CPU. A smaller context may avoid that, but this test did not measure it.

When many requests arrive together. At 32 requests, vLLM produced 2.5 times the output of llama.cpp with 32 slots and kept every first-word wait under a second. For one request at a time, llama.cpp was 5% faster and started in seconds instead of more than a minute.

Usually not. All four serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, so you change the base URL and the model name.

#10335. New OpenAI and Anthropic models sound alarms on safety and control, report

Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies.

While both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that new models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting new safety practices while Anthropic said that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.
